# About Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services LLC

## Identity
Founded in 2005 and based in Stillwater, Minnesota, Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services LLC serves clients nationwide with a concentration in Minnesota and Wisconsin. The firm's services include outsourced accounting — reviewing account reconciliations, entering transactions into QBO, reconciling bank and credit card accounts, preparing financial statements, processing bills and payments, and tracking credit card expenses and receipts — along with payroll and business tax services. Individual tax preparation is offered only to owners of existing business clients and is not promoted as a public-facing service. Slachta is affiliated with the Minnesota Society of CPAs. The firm's tone is welcoming but professional.

## Positioning & Differentiation
Slachta positions itself as "a trusted partner with niche-deep expertise — built for dentists, service businesses, and established entrepreneurs who want more than a tax preparer." Rather than framing itself as a transactional tax-prep provider, the firm emphasizes ongoing strategic support: retirement plan evaluation, collaboration with clients' personal financial advisors on financial planning, cash flow management, budgeting, and KPI tracking. Its primary contact path — a form asking whether a visitor is an individual or business owner and what they're interested in — reflects this dual focus on business clients and the individuals behind them.

## Industries Served

### Dentists
Dentists are named on the homepage as a group the firm gives "practical, strategic insight to keep you financially strong," and are reinforced in the firm's ideal-client criteria. Specific dental pain points, KPIs, and proof points are not yet detailed on the site, though the niche is treated as an active area of focus.

### Service-Based Businesses
Service-based businesses are highlighted on the homepage around a cash-flow and bill-pay angle and are reinforced in the firm's ideal-client criteria. The firm's ideal-client list names specific types within this category: Insurance Agencies, Attorneys, Architects, and Specialty Healthcare Services. Across small businesses generally, common concerns include expense management and cash flow oversight.

### Entrepreneurs / Established Small Businesses
The firm describes its role for this group generically as helping "take your established business to the next level," without specifying business stage or size beyond the general ideal-client profile. Shared needs across this group include retirement plan evaluation, budgeting, KPI tracking, cash flow management, and collaboration with clients' outside financial advisors on personal financial planning.

## Who we are

### Amy Slachta
URL: /https-//www-slachtacpa-com/who-we-are/amy-slachta

## A founder who understands small business firsthand

Amy Slachta is a CPA and the founder of Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services LLC. She built her practice around small business owners because she is one herself. Payroll runs that have to happen on time no matter what, cash flow that tightens right before a big invoice clears, the decision of whether this is the quarter to hire: Amy has made those calls in her own business, not just reviewed them on someone else's ledger.

That firsthand experience shapes how she works with dentists, service-based business owners, and entrepreneurs across Minnesota and Wisconsin. When a client describes a cash crunch or a hiring decision that's kept them up at night, Amy has usually lived a version of it herself. Clients notice the difference between an accountant who studied small business in a textbook and one who has run one.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: stillwater-minnesota-main-street.jpg | alt: "Historic downtown Stillwater, Minnesota storefronts along the St. Croix River" | query: "small town Minnesota main street downtown" -->
## Why Amy started Slachta Accounting in Stillwater

Amy founded the firm in 2005 in Stillwater, Minnesota, with a simple goal: get business owners out of the books and back to running their business. Too many owners she met were spending their evenings reconciling accounts instead of serving customers or growing their team. She started the firm to change that math.

Two decades later, the mission hasn't shifted. Slachta Accounting still operates from Stillwater, now serving clients nationwide with a concentration in Minnesota and Wisconsin. Amy's approach never treats bookkeeping as the finish line. It's the starting point for real conversations about cash flow, staffing, and where the business is headed next. That's the work she set out to do in 2005, and it's still the work that drives the firm today.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: cpa-reviewing-kpi-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Financial advisor reviewing KPI dashboard and budget spreadsheets with a client" | query: "accountant reviewing financial dashboard client" -->
## Focus areas that shape Amy's approach

Amy concentrates her practice on three groups: dentists, service-based businesses, and entrepreneurs running established small businesses. Each has its own rhythm of revenue and expense, and Amy's advisory work leans into the specifics rather than generic budgeting advice.

Across all three, a few questions come up again and again, and Amy builds her client conversations around them:

- Is the retirement plan structure still the right fit as the business and its payroll grow?
- How does this business's cash flow behave month to month, and where are the pinch points?
- What does the budget need to say for the next 12 months, not just the next tax season?
- Which KPIs actually predict trouble or growth for this specific business, and which are just noise?
- How does this fit with the plan the client's financial advisor already has in motion?

Amy treats the financial advisor relationship as a collaboration, not a handoff. She'd rather sit in on that conversation than work around it, because retirement decisions, tax strategy, and day-to-day cash management all pull on the same rope.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Credentials and professional background

Amy Slachta is a licensed Certified Public Accountant and has built her career specifically around small business accounting, tax, and advisory work rather than large-corporate audit or compliance. Since founding Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services LLC in 2005, she has focused her CPA practice on outsourced accounting, business tax services, and advisory work for owner-operated businesses.

Her client base spans dentists, insurance agencies, attorneys, architects, and specialty healthcare services, industries with distinct billing cycles, staffing models, and regulatory considerations. That range gives Amy a working knowledge of how cash flow and tax planning differ across professional practices, not a one-size-fits-all playbook applied to every client regardless of industry.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: cpa-client-consultation-handshake.jpg | alt: "CPA shaking hands with a small business client after a consultation meeting" | query: "business consultation handshake office meeting" -->
## What clients can expect when working with Amy

Clients who work with Amy get direct answers, not jargon. She asks about the business before she asks about the numbers, because the numbers only make sense in context: what's the growth plan, what's the staffing pressure, what's keeping the owner up at night this quarter.

She works alongside each client's financial advisor rather than in a separate lane, so retirement plan decisions and tax strategy stay lined up with the bigger financial picture. Budgeting and KPI conversations happen on a schedule, not just when something goes wrong. Amy treats a client's growth goals the way she treats her own business goals: worth checking in on regularly, not just once a year at tax time.

If cash flow, budgeting, or a retirement plan review has been sitting on your to-do list, Amy would rather talk it through now than after tax season. She works with dentists, service-based businesses, and entrepreneurs across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and nationwide.

### Kendra Quist

## Getting to know Kendra Quist

Kendra Quist works with the business owners who need more than a once-a-year tax return; they need someone tracking the numbers between filings. As an outsourced accounting specialist at Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services LLC in Stillwater, Minnesota, she spends her days inside the books of dental practices, service-based businesses, and established small companies across Minnesota and Wisconsin.

Clients usually come to her with the same problem: the bookkeeping is behind, payroll feels like guesswork, and nobody has had time to build a real budget. Kendra sorts through the mess, sets up a system that fits how the business actually runs, and stays involved so it keeps working after the first few months. Owners describe her as direct, responsive, and quick to explain a financial statement without the jargon.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: kendra-quist-dental-client-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing financial statements with a dental practice owner" | query: "accountant reviewing documents dental office" -->
## How Kendra supports dentists and service-based businesses

Dental practices and service-based businesses run on tight margins and heavy overhead: supplies, staffing, equipment, and the steady cost of keeping the doors open. Kendra handles the outsourced bookkeeping and payroll work that lets owners stop reconciling accounts at 9 p.m. and start reading their numbers instead.

She builds monthly close processes for dental practices that flag supply costs and production trends early, and she sets up payroll cycles for service-based businesses juggling hourly staff, contractors, and overtime rules. Because she works across both niches regularly, she recognizes patterns fast: a dentist's collections slipping against production, or a contractor's payroll creeping ahead of revenue. That pattern recognition is what turns a monthly bookkeeping engagement into an early warning system.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: kendra-quist-cash-flow-planning.jpg | alt: "Accountant walking a small business owner through a cash flow report" | query: "small business owner reviewing financial report" -->
## Her approach to payroll, tax planning, and cash flow guidance

Kendra treats payroll and tax planning as ongoing conversations, not year-end scrambles. Entrepreneurs and established small business owners she works with typically need help in the same few areas, and she builds her engagements around them:

- Setting up payroll processing that accounts for hourly staff, contractors, and benefits without errors at each pay cycle
- Building expense management habits that catch overspending before it shows up on a quarterly report
- Creating budgets tied to actual cash flow instead of last year's guesswork
- Tracking key performance indicators specific to the business, from production numbers at a dental practice to billable hours at a service firm
- Coordinating quarterly tax planning so estimated payments and deductions are handled before December, not after

She also works alongside clients' financial advisors when personal financial planning questions come up, keeping business tax strategy and personal goals pointed in the same direction.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Professional background and credentials

Kendra built her career in outsourced accounting, payroll, and small business tax work before joining Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services LLC in Stillwater, Minnesota. Her background centers on the day-to-day mechanics that keep a small business solvent: monthly close, payroll compliance, and the kind of budgeting that holds up when revenue is uneven.

At the firm, she works primarily with dentists, service-based businesses, and entrepreneurs across Minnesota and Wisconsin, applying accounting standards to the specific rhythms of each industry rather than a generic template. That focus is why dental practices and service firms tend to stay with her year after year: she already knows the questions they're going to ask before they ask them.

Dentists working with Faith get a CPA-supported team that reads a practice's numbers the way a hygienist reads an X-ray: knowing exactly what's normal and what needs attention.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: client-onboarding-documents.jpg | alt: "New business client reviewing onboarding paperwork with accountant" | query: "business owner signing documents accountant" -->
## New client onboarding documents

Starting service with our firm means a short stack of paperwork, not a mountain of it. New business clients moving into outsourced accounting, payroll, or business tax services typically need:

- Engagement letter outlining scope, fees, and responsibilities for your specific service
- New client intake questionnaire covering entity type, prior-year filings, and banking details
- Tax organizer template for gathering income, expense, and deduction records
- Payroll setup checklist, including employee count, pay frequency, and benefits information
- Request form for prior-year tax returns and financial statements

Business owners in dentistry, insurance, law, and architecture work through the same core documents; the intake questions just shift slightly by industry. Once we receive your signed engagement letter, we send the specific forms your service line requires.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: secure-client-portal-upload.jpg | alt: "Dental practice manager uploading financial documents to a secure portal" | query: "person uploading documents laptop office" -->
## Secure document exchange and portal access

Payroll records, patient billing summaries, and bank statements aren't things we ask clients to email. Every business and individual client gets access to a secure client portal for uploading and retrieving files, so W-2s, 1099s, payroll registers, and financial statements move between your office and ours without sitting in an inbox. Dentists and healthcare practices handling patient-adjacent financial data usually ask about this first, and the answer is the same for every client: nothing sensitive travels by email. If you haven't received your portal login, contact our Stillwater office and we'll set it up the same day.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: payroll-bookkeeping-resources.jpg | alt: "Small business owner organizing payroll and expense records at a desk" | query: "small business owner reviewing expense receipts" -->
## Payroll and bookkeeping resource links

Cash flow and expense tracking come up in nearly every first meeting with a service-based business owner. These recurring forms keep both under control between check-ins:

- W-4 and W-9 templates for new employees and independent contractors
- Payroll setup and change-of-status forms
- Monthly expense tracking sheet formatted for QuickBooks Online import
- Mileage and reimbursement log template
- Bank reconciliation checklist for month-end close

Attorneys, insurance agencies, and specialty healthcare practices lean on the expense tracker most, since client volume swings make budgeting harder to pin down month to month.

### Refund tracker
URL: https://www.slachtacpa.com/resources/refund-tracker

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Check your refund status quickly

Your refund is on its way to the IRS or your state's revenue department, not to a black box. The federal "Where's My Refund?" tool at IRS.gov updates once a day, usually overnight, and works for e-filed and paper returns alike. Minnesota residents can check status through the Minnesota Department of Revenue's Where's My Refund page, and Wisconsin filers can use the Wisconsin Department of Revenue's Refund 123 tool. Each system pulls directly from the taxing authority, so what you see there is the same information our office would see if we called on your behalf. Bookmark whichever applies to you and check back once a day rather than refreshing every hour. The data doesn't update that often, and repeated checks won't speed anything up.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: refund-tracker-checklist.jpg | alt: "Person checking tax refund status on a laptop with tax documents nearby" | query: "person checking tax refund laptop" -->
## What you need before you check

Before you open any refund tracker, have three pieces of information ready. Both the IRS and state systems ask for the same basics, so gathering them once saves you from re-entering data on multiple sites.

- Social Security number or ITIN for the primary filer listed on the return
- Filing status exactly as reported: single, married filing jointly, head of household, or another status
- The exact refund amount shown on your return, down to the dollar
- Whether you e-filed or mailed a paper return, since that affects which tracker applies
- Your state of residence, if you're checking a Minnesota or Wisconsin refund separately from your federal one

If you filed with our office and don't have a copy of your return handy, call us and we'll pull the numbers for you in minutes.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: refund-timeline-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing a tax refund timeline on a computer screen" | query: "accountant reviewing tax documents computer" -->
## Understanding refund timelines

E-filed federal returns with direct deposit typically show a refund within 21 days of acceptance, and the IRS tracker moves through three stages: received, approved, and sent. Paper returns take longer, often six to eight weeks, because someone has to key in the numbers by hand before the return enters the same system. Minnesota and Wisconsin generally track close to the federal timeline for e-filed returns, though both departments run additional fraud screening on certain returns, which can add a few weeks without any error on your part.

Common reasons for a longer wait include a return with the Earned Income Tax Credit or Additional Child Tax Credit, a mismatch between reported income and employer records, an address change since your last filing, or a return flagged for identity verification. None of these automatically mean something is wrong. They mean the system is doing what it's supposed to do before releasing money.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: tax-notice-review-meeting.jpg | alt: "Client and accountant reviewing an IRS notice together at a desk" | query: "client accountant reviewing letter document" -->
## What to do if your refund is delayed or incorrect

If your tracker hasn't moved in more than 21 days for an e-filed federal return, or eight weeks for a paper one, the next step is a call to the IRS or your state department directly, not a guess. The IRS refund hotline can tell you whether your return is under review or if a notice is coming by mail.

A refund that's smaller than expected is usually an offset. Past-due federal debt, state taxes owed, or child support obligations can all reduce a deposit before it reaches your account, and the Bureau of the Fiscal Service sends a separate notice explaining the amount withheld. If that notice doesn't match what you expected based on the return we prepared, don't sit on hold trying to decode it alone. Send us the notice and we'll tell you within a day or two whether it's routine or worth pushing back on.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Let us review your return while you wait

Checking a tracker tells you where your refund sits in line. It won't tell you why the amount is what it is, or whether next year's return could look different. If we prepared your return, we already have the full picture: your income, your deductions, and the reasoning behind every line.

That means when you have a question about your refund, or about a notice that shows up while you're waiting, you're calling someone who already knows your file instead of starting over with a stranger on an IRS help line. Business Tax Services and Outsourced Accounting clients get the same direct access when refund or notice questions come up mid-season. Read more about [preparing for higher taxes](https://www.slachtacpa.com/resources/quick-reads/4-steps-to-get-ahead-of-higher-taxes) if you're already thinking past this year's refund.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: cpa-team-consultation-call.jpg | alt: "CPA on a phone call with a client at a desk in an office" | query: "accountant phone call office desk" -->
## Get help from your Slachta tax team

Refund trackers are built for status updates, not conversations. If you have a question a website can't answer, call the Stillwater, Minnesota office that prepared your return, or reach out if you're a new client looking for a firm that answers the phone during filing season. We work with individuals and business owners across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and nationwide, and we answer refund and notice questions as part of the relationship, not as a separate fee.

[Schedule a consultation](https://www.slachtacpa.com/contact) and get a straight answer instead of a hold message.

## What's new in our resource library

Dentists, service-business owners, and entrepreneurs share one problem: not enough hours for finance homework. Quick Reads is where we put the short, useful pieces, articles you can get through between patients or before a staff meeting, on topics like outsourced bookkeeping for service businesses, payroll processing for small businesses, and the tax questions that actually come up in dental office accounting. No jargon, no 40-minute webinar. Just the answer, then back to work. New reads get added as the topics that matter to Minnesota and Wisconsin clients shift, whether that's a new IRS rule, a cash flow trend, or a question five clients asked in the same month.

## Tax season topics for dentists and entrepreneurs

Tax prep for a dental practice or an established small business is never just one filing. It's estimated payments, credits you might be missing, and rules that change every year. These reads cover the specifics that matter for business tax preparation for dentists and small business tax services generally.

query: tax documents calculator desk planning

### Dependent care tax credit rules for summer camp costs
photo: family-summer-camp-costs.jpg
query: parent reviewing childcare expenses paperwork

### A new way to report suspected tax fraud
photo: irs-tax-forms-review.jpg

[Read more](https://www.slachtacpa.com/resources/quick-reads/irs-gives-taxpayers-new-way-to-report-tax-fraud)

When you hand your books to Slachta, you get a bookkeeper, a controller, and a second set of eyes that catches problems before they cost you money. We work inside a secure online platform, so you can log in and see your cash position, payables, and receivables on the day you need the answer, not three weeks after month-end close.

Most outsourced accounting arrangements feel like sending your data into a black box. This one doesn't. You get monthly financials, a direct line to the person who prepared them, and a workflow built around your schedule rather than a vendor's. Business owners in Stillwater, Minnesota, and across Wisconsin use this setup to replace an internal accounting hire or to add capacity a small internal team doesn't have time for.

## Payroll handled accurately and on time, every time

Missed a payroll tax deadline once and you know why owners stop doing this in-house. Slachta's [payroll services](/services/payroll-services) cover the full cycle so nothing falls through:

- Federal and state payroll tax filings, calculated and submitted on time
- New hire reporting and quarterly compliance filings
- Year-end W-2 and 1099 preparation
- Direct support when an employee has a question about a paycheck

Dental practices and service-based businesses rarely have the staff hours to own this correctly. Outsourcing payroll to a firm that also handles your books means one team, one set of numbers, and no gap between what payroll reports and what your financials show.

## Business tax services that plan ahead, not just file

A tax return is a record of decisions you already made. The return itself doesn't save you anything; the planning that happens beforehand does. Slachta's business tax work runs year-round: quarterly check-ins on estimated payments, entity structure reviews as your business grows, and a look at upcoming purchases or hires before they hit your tax bill instead of after.

Entrepreneurs and established small business owners come to us after a few years of filing with someone who only calls in March. That model works fine until the business changes, adds a partner, buys equipment, or crosses into a new tax bracket, and the old approach stops catching what matters. Our [tax planning and preparation](/what-we-do/tax-plus) work is built to catch it, because the plan gets revisited before decisions get made, not after.

Filing still happens, accurately and on deadline. It's just not the whole job.

The same coordination applies to personal financial planning. Your business decisions affect your personal tax picture, and your advisor needs accurate numbers to plan around. We provide those numbers directly to your advisor rather than making you relay them, so the two sides of your financial life stay in sync instead of working from different assumptions.

## Accounting support built for owners who'd rather run their business

Most owners didn't start a dental practice, an insurance agency, or a law firm because they wanted to become bookkeepers. Yet somewhere between hiring staff and managing client relationships, the back office starts eating hours that should go toward the work that actually grows the business.

Outsourced accounting from Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services hands off the day-to-day financial work, bookkeeping, reporting, reconciliations, without handing off your visibility into the numbers. You still see what's happening in your business. You just stop being the one who has to produce it. Since 2005, we've built this service for owners in Stillwater, Minnesota, and across the region who want a firm that answers the phone and knows their business, not a call center that rotates staff every few months.

## What our outsourced accounting services include

Outsourced accounting isn't a euphemism for data entry. It's a full back-office function that keeps your financials accurate, current, and useful for actual decisions.

### Bookkeeping and reconciliations
icon: Calculator

Accurate, up-to-date books, reconciled monthly so you're never guessing where your cash actually stands.

### Budgeting and forecasting

Budgets built around your actual business, then revisited regularly as conditions change, not filed away and forgotten.

### KPI tracking
icon: ClipboardCheck

The handful of metrics that actually matter for your business, tracked consistently so you can see trends instead of snapshots.

### Payroll and tax coordination
icon: Wallet

Your outsourced accounting work stays connected to our payroll and business tax services, so nothing falls through the cracks between departments because there aren't any departments to fall between.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Why cash flow and budgeting guidance matter more than raw numbers

A financial statement tells you what already happened. It doesn't tell you whether you can make payroll in six weeks or whether that equipment purchase will strain cash flow through the summer. That's the gap we work to close.

Expense management and cash flow are the two issues small business owners raise with us most often, regardless of industry. A dentist watching supply costs climb and an attorney managing uneven collections are solving the same underlying problem: matching what's coming in against what's going out, before it becomes a crisis instead of a decision.

We build budgeting and KPI tracking into the outsourced accounting relationship so you're reviewing forward-looking numbers, not just historical ones. That shift, from reporting to guidance, is what separates outsourced accounting from bookkeeping.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: advisor-meeting-client-retirement-planning.jpg | alt: "Financial advisor and business owner discussing retirement plan documents" | query: "financial advisor client consultation meeting" -->
## Retirement planning and collaboration with your financial advisor

Retirement plan decisions, and personal financial planning generally, work best when your accountant and your financial advisor are looking at the same numbers instead of working from separate assumptions.

We evaluate retirement plan options as part of the outsourced accounting relationship and coordinate directly with your financial advisor rather than leaving you to translate between the two. If you're comparing a SEP IRA against a 401(k) for your dental practice, or weighing profit-sharing contributions across a growing team, that conversation happens with your advisor in the room, not after the fact. It's a collaborative model, not a siloed one, and it's how retirement and tax decisions end up aligned instead of working against each other.

### Add on services
URL: https://www.slachtacpa.com/what-we-do/add-on-services

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Extra support built around your core accounting relationship

Once your books are clean and payroll runs on schedule, most business owners start asking a different set of questions. Should I set up a 401(k) for my team? Why does my cash flow feel tight even in a good month? Add-on services answer those questions without requiring you to hire another firm or explain your business from scratch to someone new.

Think of these as modular extensions to the [Outsourced Accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting), [Payroll](/services/payroll-services), and [Tax Plus](/what-we-do/tax-plus) work we already do for you. You add what you need, when you need it. A dental practice scaling to a second location has different priorities than a solo attorney trying to smooth out seasonal cash flow, and the mix should reflect that.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: retirement-plan-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner and advisor reviewing retirement plan documents at a desk" | query: "advisor reviewing retirement plan documents" -->
## Retirement plan evaluation and guidance

Most of our business clients, from dental practice owners to insurance agency principals, don't have an in-house HR or finance team to research retirement plan options. That leaves the decision sitting on the owner's desk: SEP IRA, SIMPLE IRA, Solo 401(k), or a full 401(k) with employee matching. Each carries different contribution limits, administrative costs, and tax implications for the owner and the staff.

We walk through the tradeoffs in plain terms, model the tax impact of each option against your current income, and flag compliance requirements you'd otherwise learn about the hard way. If you already sponsor a plan, we review whether it still fits your payroll size and profit picture, or whether you've outgrown it. The goal is a plan you understand well enough to explain to your employees, not just one that checks a box.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: financial-advisor-coordination.jpg | alt: "CPA on a video call coordinating with a client's financial advisor" | query: "professional coordinating call financial advisor" -->
## Coordinated planning with your financial advisor

You don't need to choose between us and the financial advisor who already manages your investments. Personal financial planning works best when your tax strategy and your investment strategy are pulling in the same direction, and that requires someone on the tax side willing to pick up the phone and coordinate directly.

We join calls with your advisor to align on Roth conversions, distribution timing, entity structure changes, and estimated tax payments before decisions get made, not after. Advisors handle the market side; we handle the tax consequences and cash flow impact. Clients keep the advisor relationship they trust, and gain a CPA firm that's actually in the conversation instead of finding out about a transaction on a 1099 the following February.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: cash-flow-budgeting.jpg | alt: "Small business owner reviewing a cash flow report on a laptop" | query: "small business owner reviewing budget laptop" -->
## Cash flow management and budgeting support

Cash flow is the anxiety that keeps most small business owners up at night, even ones with a profitable P&L. Revenue timing, seasonal swings, and one large expense can make a good month feel like a bad one. This add-on gives you a forward-looking view instead of a rearview mirror.

What this typically includes:

- Rolling 13-week cash flow forecasts tied to your actual bank activity
- Annual budgets built from real historical numbers, not guesswork
- Monthly variance review comparing budget to actual, with plain-language explanations
- Expense tracking that flags creeping costs before they become a pattern
- Scenario modeling for hiring, equipment purchases, or a second location

Dentists and service-based businesses lean on this most heavily around payroll increases, equipment financing, and slow seasons where revenue lags but fixed costs don't.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: kpi-dashboard-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner and accountant reviewing KPI dashboard on a monitor" | query: "business owner reviewing KPI dashboard" -->
## KPI tracking to guide better business decisions

Tax returns tell you what happened twelve months ago. KPIs tell you what's happening right now. For a dental practice, that might be production per hour, collection rate, or new patient count. For a service firm, it's often utilization rate, average project margin, or revenue per employee.

We help identify the three to five numbers that actually predict your business's health, set up a simple reporting rhythm around them, usually monthly, and review them with you so the data leads somewhere. A KPI dashboard nobody looks at is worthless. This add-on pairs naturally with our [advisory services](/what-we-do/advisory-services) work, turning numbers into decisions about staffing, pricing, or capacity instead of just numbers on a screen.

### Advisory services
URL: https://www.slachtacpa.com/what-we-do/advisory-services

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Strategic guidance beyond tax prep and bookkeeping

Tax returns tell you what happened. Advisory work at Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services helps you decide what happens next. Founded in Stillwater, Minnesota in 2005, our firm built its advisory practice around a simple observation: business owners who see their numbers once a year make decisions with old information.

We meet with clients throughout the year, not just at filing season, to talk through pricing changes, staffing plans, and equipment purchases before they happen. That timing matters. A conversation in March about a hiring decision is worth more than a tax return in April explaining why the payroll number came in high.

Advisory services sit alongside outsourced accounting and payroll work, but the goal here is different: fewer surprises, better-informed decisions, and a clearer read on where the business stands right now.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: cash-flow-forecast-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner and advisor reviewing a cash flow forecast spreadsheet" | query: "small business owner reviewing financials" -->
## Cash flow management and budgeting support

Cash flow problems rarely show up as a missing number on a report. They show up as a payroll run you're not sure you can cover, or a vendor invoice that lands the same week as a tax payment. Advisory engagements at Slachta focus on catching that mismatch before it becomes a crisis.

We build rolling cash forecasts with clients so seasonal dips, slow-paying customers, and large one-time expenses show up on the calendar weeks in advance, not the day they're due. Budgets get built the same way: grounded in actual historical spending by category, then revisited quarterly as the business changes.

For an owner already juggling a practice, a client roster, or a project schedule, this is the piece that turns anxiety about the bank balance into a plan with real numbers attached.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: kpi-dashboard-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant pointing to KPI dashboard on a laptop screen with client" | query: "accountant reviewing performance dashboard client" -->
## KPI tracking and performance benchmarking

Revenue growth alone doesn't tell you whether a business is healthy. Overhead percentage, labor cost as a share of revenue, days in accounts receivable, and client retention often say more about where things stand than the top line does.

We help clients pick the three to five metrics that actually match their business, then build simple reporting so those numbers show up monthly instead of getting reconstructed at year-end. For a dental practice, that might mean production per hour and overhead ratio. For a service-based business, it's often gross margin by service line and staff utilization.

- Track overhead ratio and labor cost percentage month over month
- Monitor accounts receivable aging and collection speed
- Measure margin by service line, product, or client type
- Compare current performance against your own prior-year benchmarks, not generic industry averages

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: advisor-retirement-plan-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA and financial advisor discussing retirement plan documents with client" | query: "financial advisor client retirement planning meeting" -->
## Retirement plan evaluation and financial advisor collaboration

Retirement plan decisions, whether that's a SEP IRA, a 401(k) with profit sharing, or a cash balance plan for a dental practice, touch both business tax strategy and personal financial planning. Slachta reviews plan design and contribution limits from the tax side, then works directly with the client's existing financial advisor to make sure the plan and the investment strategy line up.

We're not here to replace that advisor or manage investments. Our role is the accounting and tax lens: what a given plan structure costs the business, what it saves in taxes, and how contribution levels interact with cash flow the rest of the year. That coordination keeps the advisor, the CPA, and the owner working from the same numbers instead of three different assumptions.

For owners without a financial advisor yet, we can point toward that conversation. For those who already have one, we join the call.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col | image: dental-office-financial-consultation.jpg | alt: "Dentist and accountant reviewing practice financial reports in office" | query: "dental practice owner financial consultation" -->
## Advisory support tailored to dentists and service-based businesses

Advisory work looks different depending on what you're running. Two niches in particular, dentists and service-based businesses, bring recurring questions that generic advice doesn't answer.

### Dental practices
icon: Stethoscope

Overhead ratio, hygiene production per hour, and staff-to-chair ratios drive profitability in a dental practice more than most owners realize until someone points it out. We benchmark these numbers against the practice's own history and help evaluate decisions like adding an associate or expanding hours.

### Service-based businesses
icon: Wrench

Pricing and margin by service line get murky fast when a business bills hourly, by project, and by retainer at the same time. We help owners see which offerings actually make money, which ones are subsidizing the others, and where prices need to move.

<!-- block: content-prose -->

Advisory conversations work best with current numbers behind them, which is why most advisory clients also use our [outsourced accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) or [payroll services](/services/payroll-services). When the same firm handles the bookkeeping, the payroll runs, and the strategy conversation, there's no lag between a decision and the data needed to make it.

Clients who only need advisory input, without handing off the accounting itself, work with us that way too. Either arrangement gives you a direct line to a CPA who already knows your numbers, rather than someone meeting your business for the first time each quarter.

### Tax plus
URL: https://www.slachtacpa.com/what-we-do/tax-plus

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: tax-plus-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Accountant and business owner reviewing tax planning documents at a desk" | query: "accountant client meeting office documents" -->
## Tax planning built around your whole financial picture

Tax Plus is not a bigger version of your annual return. It's a running conversation about how tax decisions affect the rest of your finances, from the cash you keep in the business to the retirement account you fund every quarter.

Most tax preparers file your return in April and move on until next year. Slachta built Tax Plus differently: quarterly reviews, adjustments when your income shifts mid-year, and a strategy that changes as your business does. A dentist buying new equipment, a service-based business landing a large contract, an entrepreneur weighing a new hire, each of those decisions carries tax consequences today, not just next April.

Tax Plus connects those dots before the decision gets made, not after the return is filed. Founded in 2005 in Stillwater, Minnesota, Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services has spent two decades building this kind of forward-looking relationship with business owners across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and beyond.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Who benefits most from our Tax Plus approach

### Dentists
icon: Stethoscope

Practice owners face large equipment purchases, associate buy-ins, and unpredictable production months. Tax Plus times deductions and estimated payments around those swings instead of guessing at April.

### Business Owners
icon: Briefcase

Whether you're structured as an S-corp or LLC, entity choice and salary-versus-distribution decisions shift your tax bill every year. Tax Plus reviews both before they cost you money.

### Service-Based Businesses
icon: Users

Consulting firms, agencies, and contractors deal with lumpy revenue and quarterly estimates that rarely match actual income. Tax Plus adjusts projections as jobs close and invoices land.

### Established Entrepreneurs
icon: TrendingUp

Owners with multiple ventures or a business heading toward sale need tax strategy that spans years, not one filing season. Tax Plus plans around that longer horizon.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: quarterly-tax-review-checklist.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing a quarterly tax planning checklist with a client" | query: "accountant reviewing checklist with client" -->
## What's included in a Tax Plus engagement

Tax Plus is built around five recurring pieces of work, each scheduled instead of left until year-end.

- Quarterly check-ins to review income, expenses, and any life or business changes that affect your tax position
- Entity structure review to confirm your S-corp, LLC, or partnership setup still fits your income level and goals
- Estimated tax planning that adjusts payments as your numbers change, so April never brings a surprise
- Coordination with your payroll and outsourced accounting data, so tax projections are built on real numbers, not guesses
- Collaboration with your financial advisor on retirement contributions, distribution timing, and other moves that touch both your tax return and your investment plan

None of this replaces your annual filing. It sits alongside it, feeding better information into the return you file every spring.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: business-owner-budget-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing budget and KPI reports with an accountant" | query: "business owner reviewing financial reports" -->
## How Tax Plus connects to your broader financial strategy

A tax strategy that ignores your retirement plan, your budget, or your KPIs is only half a strategy. Slachta treats Tax Plus as one piece of a larger system, not a stand-alone product.

When a retirement plan gets evaluated, contribution limits and entity structure change the tax math on both sides. When a budget or KPI review happens, gross margin and labor cost percentage become the inputs for estimated tax calculations, not a separate exercise done later.

This is where outsourced accounting and Tax Plus overlap: the bookkeeping data that drives your monthly financials is the same data that drives your quarterly tax projections. Clients who use both get a clearer, faster read on where they stand and what to do next.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: minnesota-cpa-client-meeting.jpg | alt: "Accountant meeting with a small business client in a Minnesota office" | query: "accountant meeting small business owner office" -->

## Tax planning and preparation for dentists

Annual tax prep tells you what already happened. Quarterly tax planning tells you what to do about it while there's still time to act. Slachta works with dental practice owners throughout the year on entity structure, equipment purchase timing, and retirement plan contributions, the levers that actually move a dentist's tax bill.

Business tax returns get filed accurately, but the bigger value sits in the planning conversation that happens months before the deadline, not the week of it. ## Retirement plans and financial guidance for practice owners

Choosing between a SIMPLE IRA, SEP, or 401(k) with profit sharing affects both a dentist's personal retirement savings and the tax bill for the whole practice. It's a decision that works best when the CPA and the financial advisor are looking at the same numbers.

Slachta doesn't work in a silo. That coordination matters more as a practice grows and adds associates or partners, each with different retirement needs and different stakes in the plan design. The goal is one coherent plan, not three advisors working from three different spreadsheets.

## A CPA firm built for service businesses

Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services has worked with service-based businesses since 2005, when the firm opened its doors in Stillwater, Minnesota. Consultants, agencies, contractors, and specialty firms across Minnesota, Wisconsin, and nationwide bring their accounting to Slachta because the firm treats service businesses as a specialty, not a side practice. That distinction matters. A landscaping company and a law firm both need clean books, but the questions behind the numbers differ: utilization rates, project profitability, staffing costs tied to revenue. Slachta's team works inside those questions daily, for [entrepreneurs building their first team](/industries/entrepreneurs-established-small-businesses) and established owners planning an exit.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: service-business-cash-flow-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing cash flow charts on a laptop" | query: "small business owner reviewing financial charts" -->
## Common financial challenges service businesses face

Service businesses rarely fail because of a bad idea. They fail because cash comes in unevenly, expenses creep past budget without anyone noticing, and owners have no dashboard showing which clients or projects actually make money.

The same patterns show up again and again across Minnesota and Wisconsin service firms:

- Cash flow that swings with project timing, retainers, and slow-paying clients
- Expense management that loses track of subscriptions, subcontractors, and reimbursable costs
- Budgets built once a year, if at all, and never revisited
- No KPIs tracking utilization, project margin, or client profitability
- Pricing decisions made on gut feel instead of real numbers

A firm that has seen these patterns in dental practices, insurance agencies, and law offices knows where to look first.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: outsourced-accounting-service-team.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing financial statements with a service business owner" | query: "accountant reviewing documents office meeting" -->
## Outsourced accounting and bookkeeping support

Most service businesses do not need a full-time controller. They need accurate books, reconciled every month, and a clear read on cash flow before a tight month becomes a real problem.

Slachta's [outsourced accounting service](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) handles the monthly close, reconciliations, and financial statements that owners use to make real decisions, not just file taxes at year-end. Reports come formatted around what matters for a services model: revenue by client or project, overhead as a percentage of billings, cash runway. Budgeting support turns last year's numbers into next quarter's plan, and cash flow forecasting flags a shortfall before payroll is due, not after.

For an entrepreneur running a twelve-person consulting shop or an agency with twenty years of history, that difference matters. It is the gap between reacting to the bank balance and managing toward a target. Slachta's team functions as the accounting department without the overhead of hiring one.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: payroll-processing-small-business.jpg | alt: "Payroll specialist processing paychecks for a small business team" | query: "payroll paperwork small business office" -->
## Payroll processing for growing teams

Service businesses grow their payroll before they grow anything else. A design firm adds two designers. A specialty healthcare practice adds hourly staff across three locations. A consulting practice brings on 1099 contractors for a single big project.

Slachta [processes payroll](/services/payroll-services) for teams that mix hourly, salaried, and contract workers, along with the tax filings, withholdings, and classification rules each type requires. Pay runs land on time. Quarterly and year-end filings get done without a scramble every January. As a team grows from five people to fifty, payroll stays accurate instead of becoming the thing an owner worries about at eleven o'clock on a Thursday night.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: business-tax-planning-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA discussing tax strategy with a business owner at a desk" | query: "cpa tax planning meeting office" -->
## Business tax planning and preparation

Tax preparation for a service business happens once a year. Tax planning happens all year long, and that is where the real savings show up.

Slachta works with entrepreneurs and established small businesses on entity structure, quarterly estimates, and deduction strategy months before a filing deadline, not the week of it. Contractors weighing S-corp status, consultants deciding how much to reinvest versus distribute, and agencies managing multi-state revenue all need a plan built around their own numbers, not a generic checklist.

Preparation and filing still happen, accurately and on time, but the real value sits earlier: a mid-year call that flags a tax bill before it becomes a surprise, a strategy session ahead of a big equipment purchase or a new hire. [Business tax services](/what-we-do/tax-plus) from Slachta are built to keep owners ahead of the calendar, not behind it.

## Retirement plans and financial guidance for owners

Most service business owners have more of their net worth tied up in the business than in any retirement account. That balance needs attention long before a sale or a retirement date forces the question.

Slachta evaluates retirement plan options, SEP IRAs, SIMPLE IRAs, 401(k)s, against a business's cash flow and staffing structure, and works alongside each owner's financial advisor rather than in place of one. The goal is coordination: the accounting side and the financial planning side pointed at the same set of numbers. Owners get a clearer picture of what the business needs to be worth, and what a retirement plan needs to fund, well before either question becomes urgent.

## Solving the cash flow and expense challenges small businesses face

Most small businesses don't fail because revenue disappears. They fail because cash runs out while the books still say things look fine. Expense creep, slow-paying customers, and seasonal swings can erode a healthy-looking business month by month, and by the time it shows up on a year-end statement, the window to fix it has closed.

We watch the numbers between statements, not just at tax time. That means:

- Monthly cash flow forecasting so surprises show up weeks early instead of after the fact
- Expense categorization that flags creeping costs before they harden into fixed costs
- Budget-to-actual reviews tied to real bank activity, not last year's guesswork
- Early flags on receivables aging so slow-paying clients don't quietly drain your cash

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: retirement-planning-consultation.jpg | alt: "Financial advisor and business owner discussing retirement plan documents" | query: "retirement planning meeting financial advisor" -->
## Retirement plan evaluation and personal financial planning collaboration

Business owners often have a financial advisor for personal investments and a payroll provider handling the retirement plan, and the two rarely talk. We sit at the table with both. When it's time to evaluate a SIMPLE IRA against a 401(k), or decide whether a safe harbor provision still fits the business, we bring the tax and cash flow picture your advisor needs to make that call.

The same collaboration extends to personal financial planning. A business owner's compensation, distributions, and retirement contributions affect personal tax exposure, and the reverse is also true. Rather than treating those as separate conversations, we coordinate directly with your financial advisor so the business and personal sides of your finances point in the same direction.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col | image: kpi-dashboard-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing key performance indicator dashboard on laptop" | query: "business owner reviewing financial dashboard" -->
## Tracking the KPIs that actually drive business decisions

### Margin and profitability
icon: ChartLine

Gross margin by service line or product tells you which parts of the business are actually making money, not just which parts are busiest.

### Labor and overhead ratios
icon: Users

Labor cost as a percentage of revenue catches staffing decisions that quietly outpace growth, before payroll becomes the largest line item on the P&L.

### Cash conversion cycle
icon: Clock

How long cash sits in receivables and inventory before it's usable again shapes decisions on financing, hiring, and expansion timing.

## Accounting support designed around how dental practices operate

Dental practices run on a different clock than most small businesses. Patient scheduling drives revenue, insurance reimbursements lag behind the work performed, and payroll has to account for hygienists, associates, and front-desk staff who don't all get paid the same way. Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services has worked with dentists and other specialty healthcare clients since founding the firm in Stillwater, Minnesota, in 2005. We serve practice owners across Minnesota and Wisconsin, plus dental clients nationwide who want a CPA firm that understands chairside economics as well as balance sheets. Outsourced accounting, payroll, and business tax services here are built around the rhythms of a dental office, not retrofitted from a generic small-business template.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: dental-office-bookkeeping.jpg | alt: "Dental office manager reviewing financial records at front desk" | query: "dental office front desk paperwork" -->
## Bookkeeping and payroll built for dental office cash flow

Dental offices deal with cash flow patterns that confuse standard bookkeeping software. Insurance payments arrive weeks after treatment, patient financing plans stretch revenue over months, and supply costs spike around equipment purchases or lab fees. Our bookkeeping work tracks production against collections separately, so a practice owner can see whether a slow month is a scheduling problem or a collections problem before it turns into a cash crunch.

Payroll adds its own layer of complexity: hygienists paid hourly, associates on a percentage of production, office managers on salary, and sometimes a part-time hire covering a leave. We process dental office payroll on a schedule that matches how staff actually get paid, handle the tax deposits and filings behind it, and flag when overtime or benefits costs start creeping up. Expense tracking gets tied to categories that matter for a dental practice, like lab fees, supplies, equipment, and staff costs, rather than generic line items that make year-end review harder than it needs to be.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: dentist-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Dentist reviewing tax documents with accountant in office" | query: "dentist meeting with accountant" -->
## Tax planning and preparation for dentists and practice owners

Most dentists find out what they owe the IRS after the year is already closed. That's too late to do much about it. Tax planning for a dental practice needs to happen throughout the year, tied to production trends, equipment purchases, and entity structure decisions that affect both the practice and the owner's personal return.

We prepare business tax returns for dental practices structured as S corporations, partnerships, and professional corporations, and coordinate that work with the owner's individual tax return, since practice income, retirement contributions, and personal deductions rarely sit in separate silos for a dentist. Depreciation on dental equipment, Section 179 elections for new chairs or imaging systems, and entity-level tax elections all get evaluated before December, not during it. Dental practice tax planning done early gives an owner real decisions to make, like timing an equipment purchase or adjusting estimated payments, instead of just a final number in April.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: dental-practice-cfo-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant presenting financial charts to dental practice owner" | query: "financial advisor presenting charts office" -->
## CFO and controller-level guidance without the in-house cost

Growing dental practices reach a point where the owner needs more than a bookkeeper and a tax preparer. They need someone reading the numbers and telling them what to do next. Most practices aren't large enough to justify a full-time CFO or controller on payroll, and outsourced financial leadership fills that gap.

- KPI tracking for production, collections, overhead percentage, and new patient numbers, reviewed on a schedule the owner actually looks at
- Budgeting built around seasonal patient volume, staff costs, and equipment replacement cycles
- Retirement plan evaluation, including how a 401(k) or profit-sharing plan for staff affects the owner's own retirement savings
- Cash flow forecasting that accounts for insurance reimbursement lag and financing-plan revenue
- Coordination with the practice owner's financial advisor on personal financial planning tied to practice income

## Financial support built for medical practice owners

Running a clinical practice means managing patient care and payroll, insurance reimbursement timelines, and equipment costs that don't always arrive on a predictable schedule. Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services has worked with specialty healthcare businesses since 2005, when the firm opened its doors in Stillwater, Minnesota. Physicians, specialty clinics, and healthcare service providers across Minnesota and Wisconsin, along with practices nationwide, bring us their books because they need someone who already understands how a medical office actually runs.

We're not generalists guessing at your overhead structure. Practice owners come to us with real questions: how to smooth out cash flow between reimbursement cycles, how to structure staff compensation, how to know if the practice is actually profitable or just busy. Those are the conversations we have every week with clients in this field.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: clinic-financial-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Medical office manager reviewing budget spreadsheets at a desk" | query: "medical office manager reviewing budget" -->
## Common financial challenges facing healthcare practices

Most healthcare practices we work with are dealing with the same handful of issues, just in different proportions. Recognizing them early is the difference between reacting to a cash crunch and planning around one.

- **Unpredictable cash flow.** Insurance reimbursement lag and patient billing cycles mean revenue rarely lines up neatly with expenses.
- **Expense management.** Supply costs, equipment leases, and facility overhead creep upward without a system to track them against revenue.
- **Payroll and staffing complexity.** Clinical staff, front-desk employees, and part-time providers often mean multiple pay structures and benefit tiers to administer correctly.
- **Missing performance benchmarks.** Without practice-specific KPIs, owners often can't tell whether a slow month is a trend or a blip.
- **Retirement and compensation planning.** Owners and physicians frequently postpone retirement plan decisions because they don't have time to evaluate the options properly.

Each of these is manageable on its own. Left unaddressed together, they're what push a busy, well-regarded practice into financial strain despite a full patient schedule.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: outsourced-bookkeeping-clinic.jpg | alt: "Accountant working on laptop with medical billing documents nearby" | query: "accountant laptop medical billing" -->
## Outsourced accounting and payroll for medical offices

Most practice owners didn't go into medicine to manage a general ledger. Our [outsourced accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) service takes day-to-day bookkeeping, reconciliations, and financial reporting off the office manager's desk and puts it on ours, so your internal team can stay focused on scheduling, billing, and patients.

Payroll for a medical office is rarely simple. Between clinical staff, hourly front-desk employees, and providers on different compensation arrangements, errors get expensive fast. Our [payroll services](/services/payroll-services) handle the calculations, filings, and deadlines so nothing slips through during a busy quarter.

The result is a practice that gets monthly financials it can actually read, delivered on a schedule, without adding another line item to the front-office workload. That's the point of outsourcing this work: not less oversight, just less friction.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Tax planning for specialty healthcare businesses

Tax compliance and tax planning are different services, and healthcare practices need both. Filing an accurate return matters, but so does the work that happens months before the deadline: reviewing entity structure, timing equipment purchases, and evaluating owner compensation against practice profitability.

Our [business tax services](/what-we-do/tax-plus) work through those questions with specialty healthcare clients directly. A practice organized as an S-corp has different owner-compensation considerations than one structured as a partnership between physicians. Multi-provider clinics face different questions than a solo specialty practice. We look at how the entity is structured today and whether it still fits the practice's revenue and growth, rather than treating the return as a once-a-year formality.

Proactive planning also means fewer surprises. When a practice knows in October what its tax position looks like, decisions about year-end purchases, bonuses, or retirement contributions get made with information instead of guesswork.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: retirement-plan-advisor-meeting.jpg | alt: "Business owner and advisor discussing retirement plan documents at a table" | query: "advisor client retirement planning meeting" -->
## Retirement plans and financial planning collaboration

Many physicians and practice owners put off retirement plan decisions because evaluating the options, SEP IRAs, 401(k) plans, cash balance plans, takes time they don't have between patients. We help walk through those options against the practice's cash flow and staffing structure, so the plan chosen actually fits the business rather than a generic template.

We also work alongside the financial advisor a practice owner already has. Retirement planning, investment decisions, and personal financial goals belong with a financial advisor; the tax and cash flow implications belong with us. Coordinating the two means fewer conflicting recommendations and a plan that holds up at tax time, not just on paper.

## Financial guidance built for attorneys, architects, and consultants

Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services has worked with [law firms](/industries/law), [architecture practices](/industries/architects), engineering firms, and consulting shops since the firm opened in Stillwater, Minnesota, in 2005. Billable-hour models and project-based revenue don't fit a standard small-business chart of accounts, and partner compensation structures add a layer most bookkeepers never touch. Our approach was built around those specifics rather than generic advice.

Whether a firm bills by the hour, the project, or a blended retainer, the books need to reflect how the practice actually earns money. Firms across Minnesota and Wisconsin, plus clients nationwide, bring their accounting to us when they want someone who already understands work-in-progress tracking, retainer billing, and the cash gap between invoicing and collection. That familiarity shortens the learning curve.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: attorney-reviewing-billing-reports.jpg | alt: "Attorney reviewing billing and expense reports at a desk" | query: "attorney reviewing financial documents office" -->
## Common financial challenges facing professional services firms

Professional services revenue rarely arrives on a predictable schedule. A law firm might close a large matter in March and have a quiet May. An architecture practice can carry six months of design work before the first milestone invoice goes out. That rhythm creates real strain if the accounting isn't set up to anticipate it.

The issues we see most often at firms in Stillwater, across Minnesota, and beyond include:

- Cash flow that swings hard between project completions and slow stretches
- Expense management that loses track of costs tied to specific matters or projects
- Partner or owner compensation decisions made without clear profitability data by practice area
- No consistent KPIs to measure realization rates, utilization, or margin by service line
- Retirement plan and benefits decisions made without input from both a financial advisor and an accountant who sees the full financial picture

Each of these compounds the others. Without clean cash flow visibility, partner compensation conversations turn into guesswork.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: bookkeeper-updating-financial-records.jpg | alt: "Accountant updating financial records on a laptop in an office" | query: "accountant working laptop office" -->
## Outsourced accounting and payroll for growing firms

Partners at a law firm or principals at an architecture practice didn't go into the profession to reconcile bank accounts or process payroll. Every hour spent on back-office bookkeeping is an hour not billed to a client or spent bringing in new work.

Our [outsourced accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) services cover monthly bookkeeping, account reconciliation, and financial reporting built around how service firms actually track revenue: by matter, by project, or by partner. [Payroll](/services/payroll-services) runs on schedule, whether the firm has three employees or thirty, and includes handling for partner draws, bonus structures, and benefits deductions that differ from standard W-2 payroll.

The goal is straightforward: firm leadership gets accurate numbers without doing the work themselves, and the time that frees up goes back into client service and business development.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: partners-reviewing-tax-strategy.jpg | alt: "Two business partners discussing tax documents at a conference table" | query: "business partners reviewing documents meeting" -->
## Business tax strategy for partnerships and professional entities

Partnerships, S corporations, and professional LLCs each carry their own tax mechanics, and the right entity structure at formation isn't always the right one five years later as a firm grows or adds partners. [Tax planning](/what-we-do/tax-plus) for these entities works best as a year-round conversation, not a scramble in March.

We look at guaranteed payments, partner distributions, retirement plan contributions, and quarterly estimates together, because a decision in one area almost always affects another. A partner buy-in, an office expansion, or a new associate hire all carry tax consequences worth planning for before they happen, not after the return is filed.

That proactive approach matters more for professional services firms than most businesses, since partner-level tax exposure is personal, not just corporate.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->
## Cash flow, budgeting, and KPI support for firm leadership

Knowing the firm made money last quarter isn't the same as knowing which practice area, partner, or project drove that result. Firm leaders need both.

### Profitability by practice area
icon: ChartBar

We break out revenue and cost by service line or partner so leadership can see which parts of the firm are carrying the rest, not just a single bottom-line number.

### Cash flow forecasting
icon: Wallet

Project-based and retainer revenue create timing gaps. We build forecasts around your billing cycles so payroll, rent, and partner draws don't outrun collections.

### Performance benchmarks that fit the model
icon: Target

Realization rate, utilization, and revenue per partner mean more to a professional services firm than generic small-business ratios, and we track the ones that match your practice.

### Architects
URL: /industries/architects

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: architecture-firm-accounting.jpg | alt: "Architect and accountant reviewing project financial statements together" | query: "architect meeting accountant office" -->
## Accounting built around how architecture firms operate

Architecture firms don't bill like retail shops or law offices with flat monthly fees. Revenue moves through project phases: schematic design, design development, construction documents, construction administration. Each phase carries its own billing rhythm, and work-in-progress often sits unbilled for weeks while overhead keeps running. Retainage, reimbursable expenses, and multi-year contracts add another layer that a bookkeeper unfamiliar with A/E firms can easily misclassify.

Slachta Accounting & Consulting Services has worked with architecture firm owners since founding in Stillwater, Minnesota in 2005. We understand the difference between percentage-of-completion accounting and a basic accrual close, and we set your books up to reflect how your projects actually move money. That means financial statements showing which jobs are profitable, which are eating hours, and where cash sits at any given moment, not a monthly summary that technically balances but tells you nothing useful about the business you're running.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: architecture-bookkeeping-review.jpg | alt: "Close-up of financial statements and blueprints spread on a desk" | query: "blueprints financial documents desk" -->
## Outsourced accounting and bookkeeping for design firms

Running a design practice means juggling client meetings, project deadlines, and staff schedules, not reconciling bank feeds at 11 p.m. Our outsourced accounting service handles the monthly close so you get accurate financial statements without hiring a full-time controller.

- Monthly bookkeeping built around project-based revenue, not generic small-business templates
- Work-in-progress tracking so unbilled hours and reimbursables don't disappear into the wrong account
- Financial statements delivered on a consistent schedule, not whenever someone gets around to it
- Cash flow visibility so you know what's available before committing to new software, a lease, or a hire
- Clean books ready for your banker, bonding company, or line of credit renewal

A two-principal studio and a twenty-person firm need different levels of detail. The bookkeeping scales to match your firm's size and project complexity, so you're paying for what you actually need.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: architect-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Architecture firm owner discussing tax strategy with an accountant" | query: "business owner tax planning meeting" -->
## Tax planning and preparation for architects

Architecture firm tax returns get complicated fast once pass-through income, multiple owners, and equipment purchases enter the picture. Deciding whether to expense a rendering workstation or depreciate it depends on how the rest of the year shakes out. Filing once in April and hoping for the best leaves money on the table.

We work with architects on entity structure, S-corp elections, reasonable compensation for owner-employees, retirement plan contributions, and the Section 179 and bonus depreciation decisions that come up when a firm upgrades equipment or moves offices. Licensed professionals face specific rules around personal service corporations and self-employment tax that a generalist preparer can get wrong.

Tax planning happens throughout the year at Slachta, not just in March. Quarterly check-ins mean adjusting estimated payments and making decisions before December 31, not after the return is already locked in.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Payroll services for architecture practices

Architecture firms mix salaried designers, hourly drafters, project managers, and the occasional 1099 contractor brought in for a specialized rendering or specification package. Getting classification wrong, missing overtime rules, or filing payroll taxes late creates problems that outlast the project that caused them.

We process payroll accurately and on schedule, handle federal and state payroll tax filings, and manage 1099 issuance for contractors. Multi-state payroll comes up often for firms with remote staff or projects outside Minnesota, and we set that up correctly from the start rather than fixing it after a notice arrives. Your team gets paid on time, and you get Friday afternoon back for client work instead of chasing down a payroll error.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: architecture-firm-budget-review.jpg | alt: "Two professionals reviewing budget charts and KPI reports" | query: "professionals reviewing charts reports" -->
## Budgeting, KPIs, and retirement plan support for firm owners

Numbers matter less than what you do with them. We help architecture firm owners build budgets tied to actual project pipelines, track KPIs like utilization rate, effective billing rate, and overhead multiplier, and use that data to decide whether to bring on another architect or hold steady for a year.

Retirement plan evaluation comes up often with principals nearing a transition point, and we work directly alongside your existing financial advisor rather than duplicating their role. If you already have a 401(k) provider or an investment advisor, we coordinate with them on contribution strategy and plan design so the tax and cash flow pieces line up with your broader financial plan instead of sitting in a separate silo.
